analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for brand-name drug makers to use petitions to delay approval of cheaper generic drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, despite four bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company wants to sell a cheaper copy of a drug, brand-name drug makers sometimes file 'citizen petitions' with the Food and Drug Administration that raise safety or testing concerns. The purpose of many of these petitions is to buy time, keeping the cheaper version off the market for months or years. This bill would require the FDA to weigh nine specific signs that a petition was filed mainly to delay approval, publish a public list of such petitions, refer them to the Federal Trade Commission, and allow the FDA to summarily deny petitions filed long after the relevant information became known.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay for prescription drugs, especially those who would switch to a cheaper generic or biosimilar version sooner if delay petitions were less effective. Generic drug makers, who lose sales while a delay petition keeps their product off the market, would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to consider specific factors when judging whether a petition was filed primarily to delay approval, including serial petitions, filings timed to an anticipated approval date, and petitions submitted without supporting data [S3].
Requires the FDA to publish a public list of petitions it determines were filed for the primary purpose of delaying approval, creating a public record of the practice [S2] [S3].

Requires the FDA to establish procedures to refer delay petitions to the Federal Trade Commission, which can investigate anticompetitive conduct, and lets the FDA summarily deny petitions submitted after the relevant information became known [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, which would lose a tool that currently delays generic competition and keeps their prices higher for longer.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets the FDA summarily deny any petition filed after a time period the agency sets once the relevant information became known, which could shut out late-filed petitions that raise genuine safety concerns [S3].

The bill targets only one delay tactic. It does not address other common methods of slowing generic competition, such as settlements that pay generic makers to stay off the market or patent disputes that can run for years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would meaningfully speed access to cheaper generic drugs for patients, with the cost falling on brand-name drug makers. Its main weakness is narrowness: it tightens one pathway of delay while leaving other major ones untouched, and the summary denial power could occasionally block a legitimate safety petition.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan cosponsors and referred to the Senate health committee, which never scheduled it for a vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 [S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 11, 2019 by Senator Gardner of Colorado, a Republican, joined by two Democratic and one additional Republican cosponsor [S3] [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced; that was the last recorded action [S5].
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, which keep the ability to file petitions that delay approval of cheaper generic drugs. Patients continue to pay brand-name prices longer than they otherwise would.

for.name: Cory Gardner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and recruited a bipartisan group of cosponsors [S3] [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled it for a markup or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and one cosponsor were Republicans and two cosponsors were Democrats, and there is no record of party-based opposition; the bill simply received no vote [S4] [S5].

industries.note: These companies file petitions that can delay approval of generic and biosimilar competitors, extending years of monopoly pricing on their drugs. The bill would make such delay petitions easier for the FDA to reject, shorten the window to file, and refer the worst cases to the FTC.
Generic manufacturers lose sales every month a delay petition keeps their product off the market. Faster approvals mean they can compete sooner, and their gain comes as lower prices for patients.
